citeAs: Hauret, J., Olivier, M., Joubaud, T., Langrenne, C., Poirée, S., Zimpfer, V., and Bavu, É. (2024). Vibravox: A Dataset of French Speech Captured with Body-conduction Audio Sensors. Submitted to Elsevier Speech Communication.
creator: Julien Hauret, Malo Olivier, Thomas Joubaud, Christophe Langrenne, Sarah Poirée, Véronique Zimpfer, Éric Bavu (Conservatoire national des arts et métiers / French-German Research Institute of Saint-Louis)
description: Vibravox is a GDPR-compliant dataset of French speech captured with five different body-conduction audio sensors (two in-ear microphones, two bone conduction vibration pickups, and a laryngophone) plus an airborne reference microphone. It contains 45 hours per sensor of speech samples and physiological sounds recorded by 188 participants under different acoustic conditions imposed by a high-order ambisonics 3D spatializer. The dataset includes four subsets (speech-clean, speech-noisy, speechless-clean, speechless-noisy) along with annotations about recording conditions and linguistic/phonetic transcriptions.
name: Vibravox
publisher: Conservatoire national des arts et métiers (Cnam), Laboratoire de Mécanique des Structures et des Systèmes Couplés (LMSSC)
rai:annotatorDemographics: 188 participants (97 female, 91 male). Age range: 18-82 years. Female mean age: 25.9 years (median 22). Male mean age: 31.4 years (median 27). Overall mean age: 28.55 years (median 25). A deliberate effort was made to recruit a diverse and gender-balanced group.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Phoneme Error Rate (PER) was computed for each sample using the Levenshtein distance between the labeled phonetic transcription and the phonetic transcription derived from Whisper's output. Samples with PER > 10% were discarded to ensure high-quality labels. SNR and sensitivity drift filters were also applied to verify sensor functioning.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Text for participant readings was sourced from the French Wikipedia subset of Common Voice, filtered to remove proper names (except common first names, French town/region/country names), numbers, Greek letters, mathematical symbols, and syntactic errors. Text normalization included lowercasing and removing punctuation except apostrophes. Phonetic transcriptions in IPA (33 French phonemes) were generated using the CoML lab text phonemizer. Words unrecognized by the phonemizer underwent manual phonetic transcription. Recording conditions and linguistic transcriptions are included as annotations.
rai:dataBiases: The dataset is exclusively in French, which may limit generalizability to other languages. A deliberate effort was made to recruit a diverse and gender-balanced group of participants (97 female, 91 male) to reduce gender bias. The age distribution is skewed younger (mean 28.55 years, median 25 years, range 18-82). Text sourced from French Wikipedia may introduce biases toward formal written language. The recording environment (controlled 3D spatializer) may not fully represent all real-world acoustic conditions.
rai:dataCollection: Data was collected from 200 participants (188 retained after post-processing) in a controlled recording environment using a 3D sound spatializer (spherical array of 56 loudspeakers, radius 1.07 m). Participants wore six simultaneous audio sensors recorded by a Zoom F8n field recorder at 48 kHz / 32-bit. The recording protocol consisted of four steps per participant: (1) speech-clean: reading French Wikipedia sentences for 15 minutes; (2) speechless-noisy: remaining silent for 2 minutes 24 seconds in a noisy environment; (3) speechless-clean: remaining silent for 54 seconds in complete silence; (4) speech-noisy: 54 seconds of speech in a noisy environment with in-house ambisonic recordings of concerts and street events.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Six simultaneous audio channels recorded at 48 kHz and 32-bit resolution using a Zoom F8n field recorder. Sensors include: headset microphone (Shure WH20XLR), forehead accelerometer (Knowles BU23173-000), in-ear soft foam microphone (Knowles FG-23329-P07), in-ear rigid earpiece microphone (Knowles SPH1642HT5H), throat microphone (iXradio XVTM822D-D35), and temple vibration pickup (AKG C411). A 20 Hz high-pass filter was uniformly applied to each acquisition channel during recording.
rai:dataLimitations: The dataset is exclusively in French, limiting applicability to other languages. The speech-noisy subset lacks a clean reference, restricting its use primarily to testing rather than training. Some participants had ear canals too small for the rigid in-ear microphone to achieve proper acoustic sealing, leading to data inconsistencies not always caught by filters. The dataset assumes speakers produce speech at the same loudness in quiet and noisy environments, though the Lombard effect causes increased vocal effort in noise. Body-conduction sensors exhibit inherent low-pass filtering, limiting bandwidth. The temple vibration sensor has particularly small bandwidth (below 1500 Hz).
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: The speechless-noisy subset can be dynamically mixed with speech-clean recordings to simulate noisy conditions while retaining a clean reference. For the speech-noisy experiments, static mixing of speech-clean with speechless-noisy was used. Data augmentation techniques applied during model training (not part of the released dataset itself) included speed perturbation, pitch shifting, and time masking.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Post-processing filtering was applied to the speech-clean subset in two stages: (1) Indicator extraction: Phoneme Error Rate (PER) computed using Levenshtein distance between labeled and Whisper-derived phonetic transcriptions; Lsilence_50 and Lspeech_50 percentile sound levels computed per sensor per sample using 4092-sample windows at 48 kHz. (2) Filtering: samples discarded if PER > 10%, SNR (Lspeech_50 - Lsilence_50) ≤ 1.5 dB, or Lspeech_50 ≤ Lsilence_50 (mean). VAD timestamps extended by 0.6 seconds on both sides; audio trimmed by 15 ms if boundaries exceeded. Out of 200 participants, 188 were retained; 28,471 of 30,568 sentences kept (6.8% of sentences discarded). Dataset split 80/10/10 by speaker (train/validation/test), stratified by gender.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset aims to advance research in body-conducted speech capture for robust communication in noisy environments, with potential applications in military operations, industrial settings, and emergency services. The biometric richness of body-conducted signals (capturing individual skull and timbre characteristics) opens applications in access control and intelligence gathering. The dataset was designed to be GDPR-compliant, with informed consent, anonymization, and encryption of participant data. A deliberate effort was made to recruit a diverse and gender-balanced group of participants to increase representativeness and inclusivity.
rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is intended for research in body-conducted speech processing, including: (1) speech enhancement / bandwidth extension for body-conduction microphones; (2) speech recognition / speech-to-phonemes transcription; (3) speaker verification and identification; (4) voice commands development; (5) vital sign monitoring (heart rate) using the speechless-clean subset; (6) generating synthetic datasets with realistic physiological and sensor-inherent noise; (7) comparative analysis of different body-conduction sensor technologies.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: whisper-timestamped (a speech-to-text engine based on OpenAI Whisper with dynamic time warping applied to cross-attention weights) was used for Voice Activity Detection and phoneme error rate computation during post-processing filtering. The CoML lab text phonemizer was used to generate IPA phonetic transcriptions from text.
rai:personalSensitiveInformation: The dataset contains voice recordings of 188 participants, which are biometric data. Age and gender information is included (see Table VII: age statistics by gender). The dataset is GDPR-compliant: informed consent was obtained, the purpose of data collection was clearly communicated, and anonymization and encryption of data were applied during storage and analysis.

null_reasons.rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: No external annotation platform mentioned; annotations were generated through automated tools (whisper-timestamped, phonemizer) and manual transcription by the research team.
null_reasons.rai:annotationsPerItem: The paper does not specify a number of independent annotations per item; transcriptions are single-source (automated + manual correction).
null_reasons.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: The paper describes filtering out deficient recordings rather than handling missing data per se; no explicit missing data imputation or gap-filling strategy is described.
null_reasons.rai:dataImputationProtocol: No imputation protocol described; deficient samples were discarded rather than imputed.
null_reasons.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: No versioning, update cadence, or maintenance plan described beyond the initial release.
null_reasons.rai:dataCollectionTimeframe: No specific dates or time period for data collection are mentioned in the paper.
